The steel rang through the corridor. Ada joined him, pushing at the door whenever he shouted. Sable stood behind us, pale and breathing through his nose. Nora had one hand pressed to her mouth.

On the fourth strike, the lower hinge tore loose.

On the sixth, the locking plate bent.

Rook drove the axe into the gap and leaned his full weight against it. Metal groaned. The interior bolt held.

“It’s a crossbar,” he said. “Heavy one.”

“Can you cut it?”

“Not with an axe.”

“Then take the door off.”

He glanced at the hinges. “We’ve taken one.”

“Take the rest.”

His jaw tightened. He struck again.

The workshop gave a deep, resonant thump beneath our feet. Somewhere below, a mechanism engaged. Pipes knocked in the walls. The amber lamps flickered.

“Stop,” Ada said. “The house is moving.”

“The house has been moving all night,” Sable replied. “There’s a man dying in there.”

“Or dead,” I said.

No one answered.

Rook attacked the hinges. The second tore away in a shower of rust and filings. The door sagged, but the bolt remained in place, thick as my wrist and seated inside a steel socket on the frame.

He wedged the axe between door and jamb.

“Together,” he said.

We pushed. Ada and I took the edge beside him. Sable hesitated, then added his weight. Nora stayed back, watching the broken observation panel with an expression I could not read.

The bolt screeched in its socket.

“Again.”

We pushed until my shoulder burned. The door opened a finger’s width, then two. The crossbar bent with a shriek that set my teeth on edge.

With one final wrench, the steel socket tore free of the frame.

The door flew inward.

The workshop smelled of hot metal, oil, and something bitter beneath both—sharp as crushed leaves. Rainwater had found its way through the broken observation panel and spattered the nearest papers. The brass clock stood against the far wall, its hands fixed at 11:17.

Vale lay three paces from it.

I entered first.

The revolver remained raised, though I knew how absurd it was. There was nowhere for an attacker to hide. The workshop was a long rectangular chamber, crowded with benches, cabinets, belts, gauges, and the great clock. Every corner showed itself. The window was narrow, sealed under layers of old paint, and the storm pressed against it like a living thing. The chimney opening above the furnace was no wider than a dinner plate. The only door stood open behind me.

There was no one else inside.

I crossed to Vale.

“Don’t touch him,” Nora said.

“I’m not planning to.”

But I had to know whether he was breathing.

I knelt beside him and held two fingers beneath his nose. His skin was already cooling. The pulse at his throat was absent.

“Dead,” I said.

Ada came in behind me. “How?”

I looked at the body.

There was no blood on the floor. No weapon lay beside his hand. The papers around him were torn and crumpled, but not soaked. His spectacles had fallen beneath the bench. One lens was cracked.

His right hand was clenched.

I almost reached for it, then stopped myself.

“Has anyone seen him since he entered?” I asked.

“We all saw him go in,” Sable said from the doorway. “He locked it himself.”

“Did you see him draw the bolt?”

“I saw the handle move.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“I heard the bar slide,” Ada said. “We all did.”

Rook stepped over the threshold and shut the door halfway, as if the dead man’s privacy still mattered. “There’s no one here.”

“No,” I said. “There isn’t.”

The words felt wrong. The room itself seemed to object.

I examined the floor first. The workshop boards were coated with a gray film of dust and metal filings except where the body lay. There were footprints near the workbench—Vale’s, from the narrow leather soles of his shoes. Rook’s heavy boots had marked the corridor and now the threshold. My own prints followed.

No second set.

The window had been painted shut so many years ago that the paint had cracked into a web along the frame. I put my thumb against the latch. It did not move. Salt crusted the lower edge, driven there by the storm. Even if the window could be opened, it was too narrow for a person to pass through. Beyond it, black sea boiled below the cliffs.

I examined the chimney. Ada held the lamp while I crouched beneath it. The throat narrowed almost immediately, its brick sides dark with soot. A person could not have climbed through. Not a child. Not a starving man. Not a ghost, unless ghosts were considerably thinner than the ones in church stories.

There were no concealed doors. No wall panels that yielded to pressure. No rug covering a trap. The workbenches were fixed to the floor. The cabinets stood flush against the walls.

A locked room, I thought.

The phrase had always sounded theatrical when used by newspapers. In a report, it became a problem of geometry and evidence. Here, with the hurricane screaming beyond the glass and Elias Vale dead at my knees, it felt like a verdict.

Ada pointed at Vale’s neck.

“There.”

Beneath his jaw, almost directly under the left ear, was a tiny dark mark. At first I took it for a speck of soot. I leaned closer.

The puncture was no wider than the eye of a needle.

“Is that blood?” Sable asked.

“A little.”

“Stabbed?”

“No knife would make that.”

Rook stood over us. “Could be a bee.”

“In this weather?”

“An insect carried in through the window.”

“The window is sealed.”

He looked toward it. “Then some other way.”

I touched the skin around the puncture without pressing the wound. It was already stiffening. There was no tearing, no ragged edge, no bruising consistent with a blade. A needle, perhaps. A dart. Something narrow enough to leave almost nothing behind.

I searched the floor again.

Nothing.

The clock drew my attention. Its brass face reflected the room in warped pieces: the broken panel, Rook’s shoulders, Ada’s pale face, my own hand hovering over the dead man. The second hand was still. Its tip rested just beyond the twelve.

“Eleven seventeen,” Nora whispered.

“That’s what it says,” I replied.

“And that was when he died.”

“Perhaps.”

The answer displeased her. “The impact came then.”

“The clock stopped then.”

“The clock stopped because something happened.”

“Or something happened because the clock stopped.”

Rook frowned. “What does that mean?”

I rose and went to the mechanism.

The clock was taller than I was, enclosed in a brass-and-glass case with a winding arbor at shoulder height. Earlier, its ticking had seemed irregular, accelerating and pausing as though the machine were fighting its own momentum. Now the pendulum hung motionless. I put my ear to the glass.

Silence.

Behind me, Sable said, “He was preparing a confession. Someone killed him to prevent it.”

“Someone who entered a room no one could enter,” Ada said.

“Someone who was already here,” Nora answered.

Her voice had changed. It held no fear now. Only certainty.

I looked at the others.

Sable’s face was wet with sweat despite the cold. Ada’s right sleeve was torn at the cuff, and a smear of black grease marked her thumb. Rook watched me with steady, unreadable eyes. Nora had gone very still.

The storm made the workshop walls tremble.

Then, from beneath the floor, a chain began to run.

It moved slowly at first, links dragging over a hidden wheel. The sound traveled through the boards and up my legs. The stopped clock remained fixed at 11:17, but somewhere in the house another machine was winding.

Vale had told me the confession would be read at midnight.

He had entered this room alive, carrying his ledger and his papers. He had locked the door from within. He had drawn the bolt. No one had gone in, and no one had come out.

Yet he was dead, and the only wound on him was a puncture too small to explain the fear gathering in my chest.

I bent over his clenched hand.

Between his fingers was a narrow strip of red wax.

Not the seal from the envelope. This piece had been crushed and smeared, as if he had torn it from something—or taken it from someone.

I did not tell the others.

I looked once more at the clock’s frozen hands.

11:17.

The house kept winding beneath us.

## Inspector Pike

The first thing Inspector Daniel Pike did was look at the body.

The second was look at me.

He stood in the torn doorway of Elias Vale’s workshop with rain shining on the shoulders of his dark coat, his hat crushed beneath one arm. A cut marked his cheek. Behind him, the corridor lamps shuddered as the house groaned around us.

“Everyone out,” he said.

No one moved.

Elias lay on his side beside the workbench, one hand beneath his chest and the other curled near the scattered papers. The brass clock behind him had stopped at 11:17, though my watch said 11:46. The room smelled of oil, hot metal, and something bitter I could not identify.

Pike stepped over the splintered threshold.

“I said out.”

Rook obeyed first, backing away from the doorway. Ada followed, pale and furious, one hand pressed to her torn sleeve. Sable muttered about needing air, though the corridor held only the damp breath of the storm. Nora Bell remained by the observation panel, staring at Elias as if the dead man might yet rise and contradict her.

Dr. Frost did not move until Pike caught his elbow.

“You may examine him from the corridor,” Pike said.

“I may be able to determine—”

“You may determine nothing until I say so.”

I stayed where I was.

Pike’s eyes settled on me. “You too, Miss Venn.”

“I found him.”

“That does not exempt you.”

“No. It makes me the best person to tell you what happened.”

“You’ll tell me outside.”

His grip closed around my wrist when I hesitated. It was firm, not cruel. That was worse. Cruelty could be answered. Firmness expected obedience.

I crossed the threshold, but not before looking once more at Elias’s right hand. His fingers were clenched around something pale and red—a crushed strip of sealing wax, no larger than a fingernail. I had seen it before the door came down. I had not mentioned it.

We gathered in the central hall beneath the great staircase. The hurricane had turned the windows black. Shutters covered the glass, and the manor seemed to have drawn itself inward, sealing its organs behind iron and stone. Somewhere below us, a chain began running beneath the floor, links dragging over a toothed wheel with a slow, deliberate clank.

Every face turned toward the sound.

Pike did not.

“Until the storm passes and the road is restored,” he said, “this house is a sealed scene. No one leaves the central rooms. No one enters the workshop without me. No one touches a paper, tool, clock, door, or another person unless I give permission.”

“What authority do you have here?” Sable demanded.

“The authority of an inspector investigating a death.”

“A death?” Ada snapped. “He was murdered.”

Pike looked at her. “Then you should be grateful I’m treating it as one.”

He ordered lamps and blankets brought from the occupied rooms. The narrow-faced servant appeared at the far end of the hall, pushing a brass trolley. Pike watched him place the lamps along the sideboard.

“You,” he called. “Name?”

The servant paused. “Bram.”

“Full name.”

“Bram is sufficient. It is what Mr. Vale called me.”

Pike took one step toward him. Bram wheeled the empty trolley away and vanished through a side door.

Sable gave a humorless laugh. “The house has its own ghosts.”

“It has one fewer owner than it had an hour ago,” Pike said. “Save your wit.”

Then he began taking names.

Victor Sable answered with the smooth impatience of a man accustomed to giving evidence only in rooms he owned. Ada Quill gave hers with her chin lifted. Frost spoke softly. Nora’s voice shook once. Silas Rook said his name and nothing more.

When Pike reached me, he already knew.

“Mara Venn,” he said. “Former Harbor Constabulary. Former investigator.”

“Private inquiry agent now.”

“I’m aware.”

“You came from the road?”

“From the east track. The bridge went under behind me.”

“So you reached the estate before it vanished.”

“Just. I was in the stable when the surge took the road.”

“And you heard the impact?”

“I heard it. By the time I reached this hall, Rook was breaking the observation panel.”

Rook’s shoulders hardened. “The door was locked.”

“I know.”

“It was bolted from inside.”

“I know that too.”

Pike turned to the group. “Miss Venn was the officer in charge of the Blackwater tidal-station accident three years ago.”

“Not in charge,” I said. “I assisted.”

“You signed the maintenance evidence.”

“I compiled it.”

“You altered it.”

No one spoke.

The accusation was quiet. It did not need to be loud.

Sable looked at me with sudden interest. Ada’s anger shifted direction. Frost lowered his gaze. Nora went white.

“Eleven minutes were added to the log submitted against Tomas Reed,” Pike continued. “The alteration placed him at the regulator when the emergency reversal began.”

“The alteration was discovered.”

“After his conviction.”

“Tomas Reed was not innocent.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“You didn’t ask anything.”

“I will. For now, I’m telling you that I suspected the evidence before the trial. I couldn’t prove it. The original ledger had been cleaned, and the clerk who received it disappeared before I could question him.”

“Then why did you let the trial proceed?”

His gaze sharpened. “Because suspicion is not evidence. You of all people should understand the difference.”

The words struck deeper than they should have. I understood it too well.

Pike moved toward the workshop doorway. “Miss Venn, remain in the hall.”

“I need to see the body.”

“You’ve seen it.”

“I need to examine the room.”

“You examined it enough to touch what was on the bench.”

I looked at him.

He returned carrying a square of paper between two fingers. “Your fingerprints are on the edge of the bench, the brass clock, and this.”

He held up the paper.

It was a copied page from the maintenance ledger. My handwriting. The forged page. The eleven-minute alteration appeared in the margin, neat and damning.

Ada inhaled. Nora looked at me. Rook’s expression did not change.

“You brought that here?” Pike asked.

“No.”

“It was among Vale’s papers.”

“I didn’t bring it.”

“Did you touch it tonight?”

“Not that page.”

“But you touched the bench.”

“Before the murder, during my argument with Vale.”

“About the accident?”

“About the accident, the forged log, and my brother.”

Pike’s eyes held mine. “Jonah Venn. Where is he?”

“I don’t know.”

“You haven’t seen him since he vanished six months after the trial?”

“No.”

“Did Vale know where he was?”

“Vale implied he did.”

“And you came here because of that?”

“I came because Vale promised to tell me the truth.”

“Which truth?”

“The truth about Liora’s death, the inventions he stole, and the person responsible.”

“Did he tell you?”

“He showed me a ledger. He said he would read a confession at midnight.”

“Did you threaten him?”

“Yes.”

“And did you touch him?”

“No.”

“Were you alone?”

“For part of the conversation.”

“Did you return after he dismissed you?”

“No.”

Pike stepped closer. “You understand your position?”

“I understand that your first useful act since arriving here has been to make my old crime serve your new one.”

“I have not made your old crime serve anything. You did that yourself three years ago.”

The paper in his hand trembled slightly. I could not tell whether it was the storm or me.

“Where did you find it?” I asked.

“On Vale’s worktable, beneath several loose sheets.”

“Was it folded?”

“No.”

“Was there blood on it?”

“No.”

“Wax?”

Pike looked at me.

I kept my face still. The crushed red fragment pressed against my thoughts.

“Why?” he asked.

“Vale had a sealed confession.”

“An envelope was found on the floor. Its seal is broken.”

“Not the same wax?”

“Not that I’ve seen.”

He studied me. I could not know whether he had noticed my evasion.

Pike placed the copied page inside a paper envelope from his coat. “You’ll give me your revolver.”

“I’m not surrendering it.”

“You are.”

“I’m not the killer.”

“Then you won’t need it.”

“What if the killer is still in this house?”

“Then I’ll be armed.”

His hand rested near his holster. I thought of the workshop: the sealed window, the bolted door, Elias’s puncture wound, and the clock frozen at a time that did not belong to any other clock in the house.

“If someone means to kill again,” I said, “you may need more than one gun.”

“Perhaps. But I’m not leaving a weapon with the person whose fingerprints are on the murder scene and whose forged evidence is in the dead man’s papers.”

“It isn’t in his hand.”

His attention sharpened. “What?”

I had spoken too quickly.

“The ledger page,” I said. “It isn’t in his hand.”

“I didn’t say it was.”

No one moved. Even the hurricane seemed to listen.

Pike’s voice became quieter. “What did you see in Vale’s hand?”

I could have lied. I had lied for Jonah, for Tomas Reed, and for myself. Falsehood had become less an act than a reflex, a door that opened under pressure.

“A piece of red sealing wax,” I said. “Crushed. He was gripping it.”

“Why didn’t you mention that?”

“I didn’t know what it meant.”

“You decided that was your information to keep?”

“Yes.”

“Any other details you’ve decided to keep?”

“No.”

It was not entirely true. The missing technical notation, Jonah’s name in Vale’s letters, and the things I remembered from the station remained behind my teeth.

Pike held out his hand. “The revolver.”

I drew it slowly from my coat and placed it in his palm. He checked the cylinder, removed the cartridges, and tucked weapon and ammunition into separate pockets.

Then he pointed to the settee beneath the staircase.

“You’ll sit there.”

“I’m not a prisoner.”

“Not yet.”

The word settled over us.

Pike ordered Sable and Frost into separate chairs. Ada was placed by the fireplace. Nora remained near the sideboard, hands clasped tightly. Rook chose a position against the wall where he could see every door.

Pike noticed.

“Move where I can see you.”

Rook’s jaw flexed. “I’m not going anywhere.”

“That was not the instruction.”

Rook moved.

The clocks began striking somewhere above us. Not together. One gave a thin metallic click, another answered several seconds later, and a third began a sluggish, uneven chime. They did not agree on the hour.

Pike looked up.

“What time do you make it?” Ada asked.

“Eleven fifty-two.”

“My watch says twelve-oh-seven,” Sable replied.

“Your watch is wrong.”

“The workshop clock said eleven-seventeen.”

Pike looked toward the torn doorway. “That clock is broken.”

“No,” I said.

His eyes returned to me.

“It stopped,” I said. “That isn’t the same thing.”

He considered the distinction, then took out his notebook.

“Write down everything you remember,” he said. “Before, during, and after the door was opened. Every word Vale spoke. Every movement you saw. Every person who left your sight.”

“And if I refuse?”

“You won’t.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re a detective, Miss Venn. Even a disgraced one. You know what happens when someone else controls the first account.”

He moved away before I could answer.

I opened my notebook and began writing: the time we broke the door, the body’s position, the broken spectacles, the scattered papers. I wrote that the workshop had been empty. I wrote that the window was sealed and the chimney too narrow. I wrote that the bolt had been drawn from inside.

Then I stopped.

The chain beneath the floor had gone silent.

From somewhere deep in the manor came a single heavy click.

Every lamp flame leaned toward the workshop.

Pike turned. Rook straightened. Nora made a small sound in her throat.

I looked down at the line I had begun.

The workshop clock had stopped at 11:17.

Below it, without thinking, I wrote:

Someone had wound it first.

chapters.name: The Impossible Room
chapters.content:
The workshop had become smaller since Elias died.

While he was alive, the room had seemed built to contain his importance. The ceiling rose into shadow. Brass pipes crossed the walls like veins. The workbench occupied the center beneath a green-shaded lamp, and every instrument had its assigned place, every gear and caliper and glass vial arranged with the confidence of a man who believed order was a form of ownership.

Now the room held only its dead man, its broken door, and the question of how he had been killed.

Inspector Pike stood just inside the threshold, his lantern lifted. Rain hissed against the sealed window. Beyond the observation panel, the hurricane pressed its black face to the house.

“Again,” he said.

I looked at the steel door.

“It was bolted from inside.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the answer to the first question.”

Pike’s mouth tightened. His cheek was still marked by the cut he had taken on the road, a dark line beneath one eye. He had removed his wet coat, but the smell of rain and horse clung to him. “Then tell me how a murderer got in.”

“He didn’t.”

“Got out, then.”

“He didn’t do that either.”

“Convenient.”

“No,” I said. “Impossible.”

He lowered the lantern. “You used to dislike that word.”

“I still do. But this room has earned it.”

The floor showed us what it could. Before the door had been forced, Elias’s footprints were the only marks in the thin film of dust and metal filings around the bench. He had entered alone. He had crossed to the clock. He had moved toward the worktable. No second pair of shoes had crossed the room, no wet print, no scuff, no displaced shaving of brass.

Rook had left the heavy boot marks at the threshold when he helped break the door. Ada’s smaller prints followed. Then mine, and Pike’s. All the evidence of rescue lay on top of the evidence of murder.

I crouched at the door.

The steel bolt was thick as my wrist and set into a socket in the jamb. Rook and Pike had torn half the socket from the frame when they forced entry. The bolt itself remained retracted now, its end scored where it had dragged against the ruined metal.

Pike knelt beside me. “Could it have been drawn from outside?”

“Not with this.”

“There are ways.”

“Not without leaving marks.” I ran my finger a hair’s breadth above the bolt, not touching it. “A wire would need to pass around the door or through the frame. There’s no hole, no abrasion, no bent metal. A magnet would not pull this weight through the steel plate, and even if it could, it would leave the bolt partly engaged. The socket was intact before we broke it. The bolt was fully drawn.”

“You’re certain?”

“I’ve opened enough bad locks to know when one has been opened.”

He gave me a sidelong look. “And enough good ones?”

“Those are usually more expensive.”

For a moment, the corner of his mouth nearly moved. Then the room reclaimed him.

The window was set high in the western wall, a narrow rectangle of leaded glass behind a frame painted shut. Pike had already examined it, but I climbed onto the low stool beneath it and held my lantern close.

The paint was old, layered, and cracked at the edges. Fresh salt had dried across the outside in pale, jagged fans. The storm had driven seawater against the glass hard enough to leave grit caught in the putty. I scraped one corner with my penknife. The paint lifted in a brittle curl but held the frame fast.

“If someone opened it,” Pike said, “the paint would crack.”

“It has not.”

“Could someone have come through before the storm?”

“Then the salt would not be undisturbed.”

I examined the lower edge. No fibers. No blood. No smear of grease. The window was too narrow for a broad man, and opening it would have required breaking the seal from within. Even Ada, the smallest of us, would have left her shoulders in the frame and her coat snagged on the latch.

The chimney was worse. It rose from the stone hearth in a square shaft no wider than a dinner plate. Pike had sent Rook’s lantern up it on a cord. The light had disappeared after a few feet, swallowed by soot and bends in the masonry.

I lay on my stomach and looked into the opening.

A child might have put an arm inside. A cat might have passed, if the cat were made of smoke. Not a murderer carrying a weapon, not a servant, not any human being who possessed bones.

“Unless he was poured in,” I said.

Pike’s boots shifted behind me. “Do not make jokes.”

“I’m not.”

The body had been removed to the library, but the shape of it remained in my mind: Elias on his side beside the workbench, one hand closed, spectacles beneath him, one lens cracked. The impact we had heard had been his fall, not a struggle. There had been no overturned chair, no broken instrument, no second bloodstain.

Only the puncture beneath his jaw.

I returned to the bench and studied the diagram Pike had drawn from Frost’s first examination. The wound was a neat black point under the left side of the jaw, close to the ear. A knife would have torn the skin. A narrow blade would have bruised it. A bullet would have done more than mark him.

“A needle,” I said.

Pike folded his arms. “There was no needle.”

“No.”

“No dart.”

“No.”

“No splinter, wire, or pin.”

“I know.”

“Then we are back where we started.”

I looked at the brass clock.

It stood on the far end of the workbench, tall and ornate, its case shaped like a miniature tower. The pendulum had stopped. The second hand rested at seventeen minutes past the hour. The clock face was clean except for a crescent of Elias’s bloodless fingerprints near the winding key.

Pike followed my gaze. “You think the clock killed him?”

“I think the clock may have been involved.”

“Clocks do not stab people.”

“Normally, no.”

“Normally?”

I ignored him and drew closer.

The clock had been wound with an old-fashioned square arbor set beneath the face. A small brass key remained in place, though the key had been turned slightly sideways by Elias’s fall or by the force of whatever had happened inside the mechanism. I took my magnifying glass from my pocket.

The arbor was bent.

Not dramatically. It leaned perhaps the width of a match head toward the left, where the metal entered the clock housing. But the bend was fresh. The brass around it showed a bright crescent, a rubbed place where something had pressed hard against the shaft.

I touched nothing.

“Pike.”

He came beside me. “What?”

“The arbor.”

“I see a winding key.”

“Look at the shaft.”

He bent over the clock. His lantern threw a wavering reflection across the brass face. “It’s crooked.”

“It should not be.”

“Old mechanism.”

“Old mechanisms wear evenly. This has been forced.”

“By whom?”

“Elias, perhaps.”

“Why would he wind it past the limit?”

I glanced at the clock’s face. “How far can it be wound?”

“Ask Rook.”

“Rook is not here.”

“He’s in the hall.”

“Then ask him yourself.”

Pike’s expression darkened. “You’re the one who dragged me to the clock.”

“I’m trying to understand what happened.”

“You’re trying to solve it.”

“Yes.”

He stared at me for a long moment. “You are not in charge of this investigation.”

“I know.”

“You will not handle evidence.”

“I know that too.”

“Then keep your hands off.”

I withdrew my fingers from the clock, though I had not touched it. “If you want the murderer, Inspector, you’ll have to let me look at the things you don’t recognize.”

His eyes moved to my hand, then to the clock. “And if you’re the murderer?”

“Then I’ve made a very poor choice of room.”

“That remains to be seen.”

He ordered me to step back while he inspected the mechanism. Pike was careful, but not mechanically minded. He knew a clock was a clock in the same way he knew a pistol was a pistol: by what it did, not by the parts that persuaded it to do so.

The key resisted his attempt to move it.

“That was wound recently,” I said.

“The hands stopped at eleven seventeen.”

“My watch said eleven forty-three when we heard the impact.”

“That clock was wrong.”

“It may have been.”

Pike looked at me. “Meaning?”

I pointed to the pendulum. “If it had simply run down, the pendulum would have come to rest naturally. But it stopped mid-swing. The weight is held high. The mainspring is under tension.”

“How can you tell?”

“The pendulum is not at its lowest position. It was stopped by something.”

“Something like a jammed gear?”

“Possibly.”

I lifted the lantern toward the top of the casing. A narrow seam ran along the rear panel. Near it, a smear of dark grease marked the brass. It was almost invisible beneath the dust, but the clock’s polished surface made the stain stand out.

“Was that there before?” Pike asked.

“I don’t know.”

“You saw the clock before Vale died.”

“I saw him touch it.”

“What did he do?”

“He moved papers or a tool from the bench to the clock. I couldn’t see which. Then he signaled me to wait outside.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I just did.”

“You told me he touched the clock. Not that he transferred something.”

“Because I wasn’t certain.”

“Your uncertainty is becoming a habit.”

The clock gave a tiny click.

Both of us froze.

The pendulum swung once.

It moved only an inch, then stopped. Somewhere inside the casing, a spring trembled and settled.

Pike reached for his revolver, though he had already taken mine. “Did you do that?”

“No.”

He circled the clock without touching it. The key had not moved, but the arbor seemed to flex beneath it.

Another click came from behind the face.

This one was followed by a faint metallic scrape.

I felt the hairs rise along my arms.

“Back away,” Pike said.

I did, but I kept watching.

The clock’s second hand jerked forward from seventeen to eighteen.

Then it stopped again.

Pike swore under his breath. “It’s still running.”

“No,” I said. “Something inside it is.”

He turned to me. “What is the difference?”

“A clock that is running measures time. A clock that is doing something else may be waiting for it.”

The words sounded melodramatic, but the room made them true. The workshop had the strained silence of a machine held at the edge of motion. Chains shifted in the walls. Water hammered somewhere below us. The storm pushed against the manor, and the manor answered with gears.

I looked again at the puncture diagram.

A needle. No needle found.

The bent arbor. The over-wound spring. Elias’s hand moving something to the clock. His body falling after a single heavy impact. The locked door, drawn from inside.

Not a murderer in the room.

A mechanism prepared before the door was locked.

I said it aloud. “The weapon may have been inside the clock.”

Pike’s face hardened. “May have been?”

“If it fired, it could have withdrawn afterward. Or broken. Or been pulled back into the casing.”

“And who set it?”

“That is the question.”

“Who had access to the clock?”

“Anyone who knew it was important.”

“That is not a list.”

I looked toward the observation panel, at the fractured glass and the dark hallway beyond. Every person in Vale House had a reason to hate Elias. Every person had lied. But only some of them understood machines, and fewer still understood the particular machines Elias had built into his house.

The clock clicked again.

This time the second hand did not move. A thin vibration passed through the brass casing, barely visible except where the lantern light caught it.

I imagined a needle sliding through hidden channels, waiting behind the face.

Pike stepped between me and the bench. “No one touches it until I say so.”

“Then you should have Rook brought in.”

“Why?”

“Because he can tell us what the clock is capable of.”

“And if he knows more than he admits?”

“Then you should hear his answer while the evidence is still here.”

Pike studied me, weighing whether that was advice or an attempt to draw Rook into the room. He turned toward the door.

“Stay where I can see you.”

“I’ve been doing that all night.”

He paused at the threshold. “Mara.”

I met his eyes.

“If that mechanism moves again, you do not reach for it.”

“I won’t.”

It was a promise I meant to keep.

The clock gave a soft internal shudder as he called for Rook in the hall. Beneath the workbench, something struck the floor—a small, bright sound, like a pin falling from a great height.

Pike looked back.

I looked down.

Nothing lay among the filings.

But inside the brass case, the spring continued to strain.

chapters.name: A Clock with Teeth
chapters.content:
## A Clock with Teeth

Pike set my revolver on the table between us as if it were another witness.

“Hands where I can see them,” he said.

The workshop had been cleared of everyone except Ada Quill, Dr. Frost, and me. The others waited in the central hall under Bram’s watch. Elias Vale’s body remained beneath a sheet beside the bench, its shape stark in the lantern light.

The brass clock sat where he had left it.

Its face showed 11:18.

My watch showed 11:46.

“Start with what we know,” Pike said.

“We know the clock stopped at 11:17, though Elias was alive afterward. We know it moved again after we entered. We know the puncture beneath his jaw could have been made by a needle. And we know this is the only object in the room that behaved as though it had been waiting to do something.”

Pike’s eyes narrowed. “You still believe the clock killed him.”

“I believe it may have.”

Ada leaned over the case. Her torn sleeve was tied back with linen, and her thumb remained black with grease from the earlier search.

“My father built clocks with this escapement,” she said. “None of them had a mechanism like this.”

“Everything has teeth in this house,” I said.

Pike held the lantern above the clock. Its heavy key remained in the winding arbor. The shaft was bent slightly to one side, with bright rubbing along the metal and dark grease beneath the rear plate.

“Open it,” he told Ada.

She reached into her boot and produced a narrow screwdriver.

Pike looked at her. “I ordered everyone to surrender tools.”

“You ordered Rook to surrender tools,” she said. “You didn’t search me.”

“Open it before I change that.”

The case lock had been scratched around the keyhole, as though someone had worked it impatiently. Ada turned the screwdriver. On the third attempt, the latch released.

The front panel swung outward.

The smell of old oil escaped first. Beneath it lay something sharper: bitter, green, and medicinal.

Ada’s face changed.

“What is it?” I asked.

“Nothing good.”

Inside, the clock was far more intricate than its face suggested. Wheels nested within wheels, each catching another. A coil spring filled the rear compartment. Between the winding arbor and the escapement, nearly concealed beneath a brass guard, ran a second mechanism.

“Someone modified it,” Ada said.

“How?”

She pointed to a thin lever crossing the movement. It ended in a hooked finger pressed against the winding arbor.

“The arbor turns this lever,” she said. “But the lever is under tension. See the catch?”

“What does it hold?”

“Something back.”

She removed two screws and set them on the bench. I watched her hands, afraid that one careless movement would make the clock spring open.

The lever ran toward a narrow slot beneath the arbor. Within it lay a sliver of metal, recessed in a channel no wider than a quill.

“A needle,” I said.

Pike bent closer. “Can it reach a man?”

“Not from that position,” Ada replied. “There must be a transfer arm.”

She eased the catch aside with the screwdriver.

The mechanism gave a small, hungry click.

A needle sprang forward, traveled less than an inch, and stopped against the end of its channel. Its tip was blackened.

Pike swore.

Ada withdrew the catch. The needle slid backward and disappeared into the clock.

“Retractable,” she said.

“Fires, then returns?” Pike asked.

“Projects, then returns. Don’t be dramatic.”

I ignored them. The needle’s channel aligned with a tiny aperture drilled through the clock’s rear panel. From outside, it looked like a flaw in the wood.

“Turn the clock,” I said.

Ada rotated the case until the aperture faced the workbench.

The needle’s path ended at the height of a standing man’s throat.

Pike stared at it.

“It was aimed at Elias.”

“Or at whoever stood there,” Ada said.

“Elias stood there,” I replied.

The memory came back with painful clarity: Elias lifting the clock key as he entered the workshop, holding it up as though it were part of his warning. He had not merely placed the clock on the bench. He had touched the winding arbor.

“Perhaps he knew the clock had been altered,” Pike said.

“Perhaps he didn’t know what it was. Whoever prepared it knew he would wind it.”

Ada examined the needle beneath the lantern. “There’s residue on the tip.”

Pike reached for the bell pull.

“Frost.”

The doctor entered with visible reluctance. His cuffs were wet from the rain, and his gaze went at once to the opened clock.

“What have you found?” he asked.

“Tell us what is on the needle,” Pike said.

“I need a sample.”

Ada scraped the darkened tip with her screwdriver. A minute flake fell into the paper packet Pike held ready. Frost carried it to the side table, where his case of instruments lay open.

The house groaned around us. A chain began running somewhere beneath the floor, then stopped with a heavy knock.

Frost mixed the scrap with water in a shallow glass dish. He added a reagent and watched the liquid cloud.

“Aconite,” he said.

No one spoke.

I had seen aconite once in the Harbor Constabulary’s poison cabinet. Monkshood. A pinprick could be enough if the substance entered the blood.

Pike’s expression hardened. “You’re certain?”

“Certain enough.”

“You examined Vale. Why didn’t you identify poisoning?”

“I identified no obvious cause. The wound was minute.”

He glanced toward the sheet. “Aconite can numb the skin, weaken the limbs, disturb the heart, and kill without much blood. The quantity absorbed depends on the dose and the depth.”

“Would he have felt it?”

“A sharp prick. Then burning or numbness. He might have remained conscious for some time.”

“How long?”

“Minutes. Perhaps longer.”

The heavy impact we had heard returned to my memory. Elias beside the bench. His spectacles beneath him. The papers scattered as though he had tried to seize them, or tried to write.

“And if the dose were small?” I asked.

“He might have survived.”

“Could the mechanism have delivered a measured dose?”

“Someone skilled could have arranged it.”

Pike looked from Frost to Ada. “Who here has that skill?”

“Aconite was used in electrical experiments,” Ada said. “My father kept it. So did many engineers.”

“Rook understands the mechanism,” I said.

“And Frost understands poisons,” Pike answered.

Frost’s mouth tightened. “I have treated poisoned men. That is not the same as poisoning them.”

“No,” I said. “But it is closer than most people get.”

Pike ignored the exchange and returned to the clock. “How is the needle triggered?”

Ada pointed to the lever. “Winding the arbor draws it back and engages the catch. The spring holds it there. If the catch releases, the lever drives the rod forward.”

“What releases it?”

“The movement may do so after a delay. The arbor was forced beyond its limit. The pendulum was arrested, perhaps to hold the mechanism in readiness.”

“Then it could have fired at 11:17,” Pike said.

“Not necessarily,” Ada replied. “It moved after we entered.”

“It may have fired earlier and retracted later.”

“Why stop the clock?”

“To make us believe 11:17 was the time of death.”

Ada shook her head. “The movement might have stopped naturally after firing.”

“Unless the stop was part of the design,” I said.

Pike turned to me.

“The clock was wound beyond its limit. The needle was held under tension. The pendulum was locked. Whoever made it wanted the mechanism to wait for a chosen action.”

“Chosen by whom?” Ada asked.

I looked at the bent arbor.

“By Elias.”

Pike frowned.

“Elias entered alone,” I said. “He locked the door and drew the bolt. If the clock was prepared beforehand, the killer never needed to enter after him. Elias only had to do what he always did—wind the clock, or attempt to correct it.”

Ada nodded slowly. “The winding motion could release the catch.”

“Or the clock could have been set to release once the spring reached a particular tension.”

Pike studied the mechanism. “How would the killer know where Vale would stand?”

“He knew the workshop,” Ada said.

“He knew Vale’s habits,” I added. “He knew Vale would carry the clock inside. He knew the confession would keep him there.”

Frost looked toward the covered body. “Mr. Vale arranged his own drama.”

“He arranged a false death, perhaps,” I said. “Aconite might have been intended to make him appear dead, then leave him conscious enough to deliver his confession.”

Pike’s eyes sharpened. “You think he planned this?”

“I think he moved papers from the bench toward the clock before he locked the door. I think he expected the clock to matter. And I think someone altered the dose or the trigger so he died before he could speak.”

Frost said nothing.

The silence was answer enough to make me look at him.

Pike stepped between us. “We will test every bottle in the house. Until then, nobody touches this clock.”

He looked at me as he said it.

I looked back at the narrow channel where the needle had vanished. There was no weapon in the room, no dropped dart, no loose fragment of metal for a guilty hand to hide. The puncture had been made by something that could strike and withdraw before anyone entered.

The locked room had not been opened.

It had been prepared.

And somewhere among us was the person who knew Elias Vale’s habits well enough to turn time itself against him.

chapters.name: The First Lies
chapters.content:
### The First Lies

Pike put us in the central hall beneath the dead chandelier and questioned us one at a time.

The storm had made a prison of Vale House, but it was not the walls that held us. It was suspicion. We sat in a rough semicircle while rain struck the windows like thrown gravel, each of us watching the others for the movement that might become a confession.

Pike had taken my revolver. He had also taken the clock apart far enough to prove that it could have killed Elias, but not far enough to tell us who had taught it to do so. The modified mechanism sat on a table in the workshop under a sheet, like a corpse awaiting burial.

“Until the roads reopen,” Pike said, “nobody leaves this hall without my permission. Nobody enters the workshop. Nobody handles a tool, bottle, paper, or piece of machinery without telling me.”

Victor Sable gave a thin, humorless smile. “You make it sound as though the house itself is under arrest.”

“It may be,” Pike said.

At that moment, something deep below us engaged with a heavy clank. The floor trembled beneath our feet. Ada Quill looked toward the corridor. Nora Bell flinched. Rook did neither.

Pike noticed.

“So,” he said. “We begin with the hours before Vale entered the workshop. Mr. Sable, you first.”

Sable rose with the offended dignity of a man accustomed to being questioned only by shareholders. He was broad through the shoulders, silver-haired, and dressed in a dinner jacket too fine for the weather. A dark smear marked one cuff. He had tried to wipe it away, but the grease had settled into the cloth.

Pike led him to the far end of the hall, where the tiled floor gave a clear view of every door. I remained seated, though I angled myself to see both men in the mirror over the fireplace.

“Tell me where you were between nine and eleven,” Pike said.

“In the dining room for part of it. Then in the west salon.”

“Alone?”

“For most of the time.”

“Most?”

Sable sighed. “I spoke with Vale in his study.”

“About?”

“Business.”

“Be specific.”

Sable looked at the rain-streaked glass. “Money had gone missing from two of the Vale companies. Transfers made through a shell concern in Rotterdam. I asked him to explain.”

“And did he?”

“He accused me of stealing it.”

“Were you?”

“I moved funds at his instruction.”

“Did you move funds to silence anyone connected with Liora Vale’s death?”

Sable’s jaw tightened. “I arranged payments. That is not the same thing.”

“To whom?”

“To men who would otherwise have brought claims against the company. Dock inspectors. A solicitor. A family who wanted a settlement.”

“Tomas Reed’s family?”

Sable did not answer at once.

That was answer enough.

“Did you threaten Elias?” Pike asked.

“I told him his fortune was built on paper thin enough to burn. He told me he intended to read his confession at midnight and let the ashes fall where they might.”

“Did you follow him to the workshop?”

“No.”

Ada made a low sound from her chair. Sable turned toward her.

“You were there,” she said.

Sable’s expression went blank. “I was not.”

“I saw you near the gallery doors.”

Pike’s head shifted. “Mr. Sable?”

Sable rubbed his mouth. “I went as far as the gallery. I wanted the account books from the display room. Vale had them locked with the patent files.”

“Did you enter?”

“No.”

“Why did you lie?”

“Because I knew what it would look like.”

“It looks like you had a reason to kill him.”

“Everyone here had a reason.”

Pike let him sit. Sable returned to his chair with the careful stiffness of a man who had just discovered that the room was smaller than it appeared.

Ada was next.

She rose before Pike called her name. Her torn sleeve brushed the arm of her chair. The black crescent beneath her thumb had not come clean, despite repeated scrubbing.

“I entered the display room,” she said.

Pike’s eyes narrowed. “When?”

“Shortly after dinner. I was there perhaps ten minutes.”

“What were you looking for?”

“Proof.”

“Of?”

“That Vale stole my father’s work.”

The words struck harder than Sable’s admission. Ada had accused Elias openly at dinner, but there was a difference between accusation and trespass. Her father, Martin Pell, had died with creditors at his door and a regulator design in his desk that later appeared, perfected and patented, under Vale’s name.

“What did you find?” Pike asked.

“Cabinets of drawings. Purchase agreements. Nothing I could remove without being noticed.”

“Did you touch the brass clock?”

“No.”

“Did you touch anything in the workshop?”

She hesitated.

Pike saw it. I saw it too.

“I crossed the gallery,” she said. “The workshop door was already shut.”

“That isn’t my question.”

“I put my hand on the observation panel.”

“Why?”

“To see whether Vale was inside.”

“Was he?”

“Yes.”

“What was he doing?”

“Moving papers. He took something from the bench to the clock.”

“What?”

“A tool, perhaps. Or a key. I couldn’t tell.”

“Did he see you?”

“He looked toward the glass.”

“Did you speak?”

“He raised one finger. Wait.”

That matched my own memory, though I had not told Pike that Vale had made the same gesture to me. I had thought it meant patience. Now it seemed more like command.

“Why didn’t you tell me about the display room before?” Pike asked.

“Because my father’s name is all I have left. If Vale had hidden proof of the theft, I meant to take it before he destroyed it.”

“Did you find aconite there?”

“No.”

“Would you know where to obtain it?”

“My father used it in experiments.”

“Many engineers did.”

“Then perhaps you should ask an engineer.”

Her gaze slid toward Rook. He sat with his hands folded between his knees, his face impassive.

Pike dismissed her. As she passed me, I saw a thin red mark across her palm, as though she had gripped something sharp.

“Your turn, Miss Bell,” Pike said.

Nora did not move.

She had been sitting nearest the library door, pale and straight-backed, with her hands clasped so tightly that the knuckles showed white. When Pike called her, she rose as if pulled by a wire.

“Tell me about Liora,” he said.

Nora looked at the covered clock on the table. “What about her?”

“You served as Mr. Vale’s secretary. You were close to his wife.”

“Not his wife.”

“Close to Liora.”

“Yes.”

“Did she intend to leave Blackwater?”

“Yes.”

“Did she intend to expose Elias?”

“Yes.”

“Did she find something in the tidal tunnels?”

Nora’s lips parted. For several seconds only the storm answered.

“She found drawings,” she said at last. “Old ones. Plans for the regulators beneath the cliffs.”

“Whose plans?”

“Her father’s, perhaps. My father’s. Martin Pell’s. Liora believed the designs had been taken from several inventors and assembled here.”

“Why did she go into the tunnels?”

“To retrieve a case of papers.”

“Did she tell you what was in it?”

“No.”

“Did you warn her not to go?”

“I warned Elias.”

That drew all our attention.

Nora’s eyes fixed on Pike. “That evening. Before the accident. I told him Liora had found something in the tunnels and that she meant to publish it.”

“What did he say?”

“He said she was frightened and confused.”

“Did he know where she was?”

“Yes.”

“Did you?”

“I knew she had gone below the station.”

“Who went after her?”

Nora shook her head. “I don’t know.”

“You were there.”

“I was in the office.”

“Did you hear an argument?”

Her face changed—not much, but enough. A tightening around the eyes. A breath held too long.

“I heard Liora shouting.”

“At whom?”

“I couldn’t make out the words.”

“Could you make out the other voice?”

Nora looked at me then. Not at Pike. At me.

“Yes,” she said. “A man’s.”

“Whose?”

“I don’t know.”

It was a lie, or close enough to one that the difference did not matter.

“Did you tell the police that?”

“I told Dr. Frost.”

“Dr. Frost altered the medical report.”

“I know.”

“And you kept silent?”

“I was afraid.”

“Of Elias?”

Nora’s gaze moved to the workshop corridor. “Of what the truth would do to everyone.”

Pike let that sit between us. Then he sent her back.

Rook was the last before Frost.

He rose slowly, with the awkwardness of a man whose body had been assembled for labor rather than conversation. His boots were still wet at the edges. There was a nick in the leather of the right one, exposing gray beneath the black polish.

“You worked on the clock tower today,” Pike said.

“On the tower drive.”

“What does that mean?”

“The tower’s main weight was slipping. I repaired the brake and reset the governor.”

“Did you work on the brass clock in the workshop?”

“No.”

“Have you ever worked on it?”

“I’ve serviced the casing. Not the movement.”

“You helped break down the workshop door.”

“It was necessary.”

“You knew where to strike.”

“I know doors.”

Pike stepped closer. “The clock’s winding arbor was bent. Its rear panel had been opened recently. The mechanism contains a retractable needle coated in aconite. Someone modified it with mechanical skill.”

Rook’s face remained still, but the muscles at his throat moved.

“There are other mechanics in the world,” he said.

“Name one with access to this house.”

“Me. Bram, if he’s still skulking about. Mr. Vale himself.”

“And you?”

“I didn’t touch the clock.”

“Where were you before Vale entered the workshop?”

“Checking the tower.”

“Who saw you?”

“No one.”

“Convenient.”

“It’s a tower, Inspector. People don’t climb it for company.”

“Did you go down by the tidal stairs?”

Rook looked at him then. “No.”

Ada turned sharply. “I saw you there.”

Rook’s eyes went to her. “You saw a man in a dark coat.”

“I saw you.”

“Then why didn’t you say so before?”

“Because I wasn’t asked.”

Pike’s attention moved between them. “Mr. Rook, did you go to the tidal stairs?”

Rook considered the question, which was not the same as considering the truth.

“Yes,” he said. “Briefly.”

“Why lie?”

“Because I knew you’d make it important.”

“It is important.”

“I checked a sluice control. The pressure in the lower pipes had changed.”

“Changed how?”

“Rising.”

The house gave another deep mechanical groan, as if in agreement.

“Did you alter it?”

“No.”

“Did you see anyone?”

“No.”

“Did you touch the clock?”

“No.”

There it was again. The same answer, polished and placed carefully between us.

Pike sat back. “You know the house better than any of us. You maintain its hidden systems. You had opportunity to prepare the clock.”

“So did Vale.”

“Did Vale know about the needle?”

“I don’t know.”

“Did he know about the poison?”

“I don’t know.”

“Did he ask you to repair anything in the workshop?”

“No.”

“What did he ask you to do?”

Rook’s gaze settled on the sheet covering the clock. “Keep the house running.”

“Why?”

“Because he built it to run.”

Pike dismissed him.

Frost remained seated.

He had not looked at the dead man since we found him. His hands rested on the arms of his chair, fingers relaxed, but his right thumb kept rubbing the side of his forefinger. A physician’s habit, perhaps. Or a man trying to remove a stain that was not there.

“Doctor,” Pike said, “you examined Liora Vale after the accident.”

“I did.”

“Your report stated that she died instantly.”

“Yes.”

“You now admit she inhaled water.”

“I said the report was incomplete.”

“Incomplete enough to erase eleven minutes?”

Frost’s mouth compressed. “The injuries were catastrophic. Any survival would have been brief and meaningless.”

“Meaningless to whom?”

“To the dead.”

“To Liora, perhaps.”

The doctor looked at me. “You were not there.”

“No,” I said. “I was only the officer who wrote down what everyone told me.”

“And changed it.”

Pike’s expression sharpened, but I held Frost’s gaze.

“Did Elias order you to alter the report?” Pike asked.

“He instructed me to keep speculation out of it.”

“Did he pay you?”

“He paid me for medical services.”

“Did he threaten you?”

“No.”

“Did Liora have water in her lungs?”

“Yes.”

“Could she have spoken?”

“I cannot say.”

“Could she have identified the person with her?”

“I cannot say.”

“Could she have lived eleven minutes?”

Frost’s thumb stopped moving.

“The question is not useful,” he said.

“It is the question I asked.”

“Then yes. Possibly.”

The hall seemed to contract around us.

“Was there another voice at the station?” Pike asked.

Frost’s eyes lowered. “There may have been.”

“Whose?”

“I don’t know.”

“You told Miss Bell you knew the truth.”

“I told her the accident was complicated.”

“Was it an accident?”

Frost looked toward the covered workshop door. His face had gone gray.

“Yes,” he said. “Liora Vale’s death was an accident.”

The answer came too quickly. Not with conviction, but with preparation.

Pike leaned forward. “And Elias’s?”

Frost did not reply.

A chain began moving somewhere in the walls. It dragged for three links, stopped, then dragged again. Every head turned toward the sound.

Rook was watching Frost.

Frost was watching the workshop.

And I was watching the clock beneath its sheet, where something small and hard clicked once, like a tooth closing on bone.

chapters.name: The Tidal Mark
chapters.content:
## The Tidal Mark

The covered clock clicked once more.

No one spoke.

The sound had come from the workshop beyond the sealed doors, faint but distinct beneath the thunder. It was not the uncertain stutter of a damaged spring. It was the clean, final sound of a catch settling into place.

Inspector Pike lifted his head.

“Did anyone touch it?”

We were all in the central hall, arranged beneath the dead chandelier like figures in a tableau painted by a cruel artist. Sable sat rigidly on the settee, his damp cuffs dark against his knees. Ada stood near the fireplace with her arms folded, though the thin red mark across her palm showed whenever the firelight caught it. Nora Bell had retreated beside the grandfather clock, pale and watchful. Dr. Frost remained near the doors to the gallery.

Rook was the only one who looked toward the workshop without surprise.

“I didn’t,” he said.

“That wasn’t the question,” Pike replied. “Did anyone touch it?”

“No.”

Pike’s gaze moved from face to face. Then it settled on me.

I had learned, in my former profession, that silence was not the absence of evidence. It was evidence with its coat buttoned.

“I heard the click,” I said. “I was here.”

“So was everyone else.”

The hurricane struck the manor broadside. Windows trembled in their frames, and somewhere above us a chain ran rapidly through a guide, links clattering with such violence that Nora flinched. The house seemed to be thinking. Or counting.

Pike crossed to the workshop doors and pressed his ear against the steel.

“The room is still sealed,” he said.

“Sealed rooms don’t kill men,” Sable muttered. “People do.”

“People who know how to make rooms appear sealed,” Ada said.

Rook glanced at her. “You’ve been reading too many adventure novels.”

“I’ve been reading the mechanism.”

Pike took the lantern from the table. “No one leaves the hall. No one touches any machinery. I’m going to check the workshop observation panel again.”

He turned away, and I saw Rook’s right hand close around something in his coat pocket.

Not a weapon. The outline was too narrow, too familiar.

A screwdriver, perhaps.

I watched him until he noticed.

“What?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

“That’s a poor habit for an investigator.”

“I’m out of practice.”

The lie sat between us. I was not out of practice. I had simply spent three years practicing the wrong thing.

Pike returned after several minutes, wetter than before. He had examined the broken observation panel without entering the workshop. The steel door remained wedged open by the brace we had driven beneath it, and the bolt still lay on the floor where it had fallen when we tore the door from its hinges.

“The clock has not moved,” he said. “The hands remain at eleven seventeen.”

“Your watch says eleven forty-three,” Ada reminded him.

“Thirty-nine now.”

“The clock stopped before Vale died,” Sable said. “That much is obvious.”

“Is it?” I asked.

He looked at me with irritation. “The dead man was beside it.”

“Then why did it jerk forward when Pike touched the arbor?”

Pike’s mouth tightened. “Because someone damaged it.”

“Or because it was designed to respond.”

Rook gave a short laugh. “Designed to respond to what?”

I looked at him. “That’s what I intend to find out.”

Pike did not like the exchange, but he disliked the clock more. He led us back to the workshop threshold, where the lantern light fell across Elias Vale’s body beneath the sheet. The workshop smelled of hot metal, rain, and the bitter medicinal trace of aconite. Nothing moved except the flame.

The brass clock stood on the bench, its pendulum arrested. Its rear casing was open where we had examined the hidden needle. A narrow channel ran from the winding arbor to the recessed mechanism. I crouched beside it.

“Hold the lantern lower,” I said.

Pike did.

At first I saw only brass dust and a dark line along the underside of the casing. Then I noticed the smear.

It lay where the clock’s rear panel met the bench, no wider than my little finger, black and glossy in the light.

I touched it with the tip of a clean matchstick.

The substance stretched.

“Grease,” Pike said.

“Not ordinary grease.”

Rook stood behind us. “There are a dozen kinds in this house.”

“Name this one.”

He did not answer at once.

I rose and held the matchstick toward him. The grease glistened like tar.

“Marine bearing compound,” he said finally. “Used on submerged gears, sluice pivots, anything exposed to salt water.”

“Common throughout the manor?”

“Common enough.”

“Then it should be on the clock.”

“It may have been dragged there.”

“By whom?”

“By anyone who has worked on the machinery.”

Pike reached for the matchstick, then stopped himself. He used a handkerchief to take it instead.

“Where is this particular machinery?” he asked.

Rook shrugged. “Under the cliffs. Old tidal engines. Most of them abandoned.”

“You’ve been there tonight?”

“No.”

“Ada saw you near the tidal stairs.”

“I went to check the pressure.”

“Which required marine grease?”

“Not tonight.”

I looked again at the black smear. It was beneath the casing, not on the floor. A hand carrying grease would have marked the outside of the clock first. This had been applied while the panel was open, when someone had reached into its guts.

The same person who had adjusted the needle.

I leaned closer. The trigger was a thin steel finger seated behind the transfer arm. There, along its edge, was a small crescent of disturbed metal. The screw head beside it showed fresh scoring.

“Pike.”

He brought the lantern around.

“The adjustment screw,” I said. “Look at the nick.”

A triangular gouge cut across the rim of the head. Not a random scratch. Three clean sides, like a tiny bite.

Rook stepped forward. “What about it?”

“This was turned recently.”

“By a screwdriver.”

“Yes.”

“Most screwdrivers leave marks.”

“Not that mark.”

I reached toward the tool roll Pike had confiscated from the bench earlier, then remembered his order and withdrew my hand.

Rook’s expression hardened. “You’ll need a comparison.”

“I know.”

Pike looked at him. “Your tools.”

“They’re in the satchel by the hall.”

“Fetch them.”

“I thought no one was to leave.”

“I’ll fetch them,” Pike said.

Rook’s eyes flicked toward the door, toward the rain-blurred gallery beyond it. In that instant I saw not fear, but calculation. Then he nodded.

His satchel had been left under a chair in the central hall. Pike retrieved it himself and brought it to the workshop threshold. The leather was stained with salt and blackened at the seams. He opened it on the floor.

Wrenches. Pliers. A file. Two awls. A folding rule. Three screwdrivers.

The largest was Rook’s favorite, he told us before anyone asked. Its handle was made of dark wood polished smooth by years of use. Near the tip, one corner of the blade bore a triangular nick.

Pike took it with a handkerchief and held it beside the clock’s adjustment screw.

The mark fit.

Not perfectly. Nothing ever did in a world where metal wore down and men lied. But the three-sided bite was unmistakable.

Nora made a small sound.

Rook’s face remained still.

“That proves possession,” he said. “Not murder.”

“It proves your screwdriver was used on the trigger,” Pike answered.

“No. It proves a screwdriver with a damaged blade made that mark. There are other mechanics in Blackwater.”

“Name one here.”

“Bram.”

The unidentified servant’s name—or the only name he allowed us—fell into the room.

“Bram has worked on these systems for years,” Rook continued. “He handles tools. He could have borrowed mine.”

“Could he?” I asked.

Rook looked at me. “You know he could.”

I did know it. Bram had passed through the manor all evening without belonging to any room in it. I had seen him carrying coal, a tray, a coil of wire. I had not seen him now for nearly an hour.

“Where is he?” Pike asked.

“Probably securing the lower shutters.”

“Then why hasn’t he reported to me?”

“Because he doesn’t report to anyone.”

Pike wrapped the screwdriver in cloth and placed it beside the grease sample.

“Who else has access to your tools?”

“Anyone who can open a satchel.”

“Was it locked?”

“No.”

“Were you with it when Vale entered the workshop?”

Rook’s gaze shifted toward the clock. “It was in the hall.”

“You were near the tidal stairs.”

“I told you why.”

“And before that?”

“On the gallery.”

“Doing what?”

“Watching the storm.”

“That’s not what Ada said.”

Rook turned to Ada. “What did you say?”

“That I saw you come from the direction of the stairs.”

“Did you see me touch the clock?”

“No.”

“Did you see me enter the workshop?”

“No.”

“Then you saw a man walking through a house.”

Ada’s jaw tightened. “A man who lied about where he had been.”

“So did you.”

“I never claimed to be innocent.”

The admission silenced him for a moment.

I crouched again by the clock. The grease had gathered in a narrow crescent beneath the lower hinge, where a hand would rest while loosening the rear casing. I imagined the killer opening the panel, fitting the spring, bending the arbor, testing the needle. Someone had worked carefully. Someone had known precisely how far the mechanism must be set.

And afterward, someone had wiped the clock clean—almost.

Why leave the grease?

Because it had been overlooked. Because the killer had hurried. Or because it was meant to be found.

A staged clue could be more dangerous than no clue at all.

Pike was looking at Rook’s hands. “You have grease under your fingernails.”

Rook glanced down. Black stained the beds of two nails on his left hand.

“From the tower drive,” he said. “I told you. The main weight is slipping.”

“Show me.”

“Here?”

“Now.”

Rook’s mouth drew thin. “The tower is not safe.”

“Neither is this room.”

Lightning turned the workshop white. For an instant, the clock’s brass face reflected us all: Pike, broad and grim; Ada with her hand pressed against her side; Sable shrinking into his expensive coat; Nora standing as if she expected the walls to accuse her; Frost motionless near the door; Rook at the center of the reflection, his image split by the clock hands.

Eleven seventeen.

I remembered his expression when the clock had stopped. Not surprise. Recognition.

“Rook,” I said, “when the impact came, you knew what it was.”

“I knew a mechanism had failed.”

“You said that before we saw Vale.”

“I heard metal.”

“It was a heavy impact.”

“In a house full of machinery, everything sounds like an impact.”

“Not to you.”

His eyes met mine. They were a gray so pale they almost disappeared beneath the workshop’s dimness.

“You’ve decided,” he said.

“I’ve noticed.”

“That’s the same thing with less courage.”

Pike stepped between us. “You will remain in the central hall until I say otherwise.”

“I have done nothing.”

“No one here has done nothing,” Pike said.

A deep vibration passed through the floor.

It began under our boots and traveled upward through the walls, a slow pressure like a giant hand closing around the foundations. The lamps guttered. From somewhere below came the muffled rush of water.

Rook’s head turned toward the sound.

Not toward the nearest drain or the windows.

Toward the tidal stairs.

I saw it. So did Pike.

“What was that?” Nora whispered.

“The lower sluice,” Rook said.

“Why would it open?” Ada asked.

“It may have been triggered by the storm.”

“Can you stop it?”

Rook hesitated.

That hesitation was the first honest thing I had seen from him.

Pike seized his arm. “You’re coming with me.”

Rook pulled free, not violently, but with enough strength to make the movement a warning. “If the pressure is rising, you’ll want someone who understands the system.”

“I want someone who understands the system and can be watched.”

“Then watch me.”

Pike pointed to the hall. “Move.”

Rook obeyed. As he passed me, the smell of his coat reached me: wet wool, iron, and the same black marine grease that gleamed beneath the clock casing.

It might have come from the tower.

It might have come from the tidal stairs.

It might have come from the hidden hand that had prepared Elias Vale’s death.

I looked at the triangular nick in the screwdriver, then at Rook’s retreating back.

A mark was not a verdict. I knew that better than anyone.

Three years earlier, I had made a mark into a verdict with eleven false minutes.

Behind us, beneath the sheet, the brass clock clicked again. This time it sounded less like a dying machine than a lock turning.

And somewhere below the house, water began to move.

chapters.name: The Accident
chapters.content:
## The Accident

Pike gave me the central hall, the dead chandelier, and the six people who had lied about Liora Vale.

He gave me twenty minutes.

“Separately,” he said. “You ask. I listen.”

Rain hammered the shutters. Somewhere below us, a chain dragged through the walls with a long metallic groan, then stopped. Every face in the hall turned toward the sound.

Rook’s was the only one that did not.

He stood near the fireplace with his arms folded, his damp hair combed back from a forehead marked by a thin white scar. The inspector had taken his screwdriver and locked it in the evidence case. Without it, Rook looked less like a mechanic and more like a man who had been deprived of a weapon.

Pike touched my elbow. “Start with Frost.”

The doctor sat beneath the portrait of Elias Vale, his hands clasped over the head of his cane. He had not looked at the body since we found it. He had not looked at the clock either.

I led him into the adjoining morning room, where the windows rattled in their frames and the fire had burned low.

“You falsified Liora’s report,” I said.

His fingers tightened on the cane. “That is a harsh way to begin.”

“It is an accurate one.”

“Accuracy has become a fashionable word in this house.”

I placed my hands on the back of a chair but did not sit. “Her death was recorded as instantaneous. You wrote that she died on contact with the water.”

“She fell beneath the regulator gantry. The machinery was collapsing. It was dark, chaotic—”

“Was she dead when you reached her?”

His eyes moved to the rain-streaked glass. “No.”

The answer landed more heavily than a confession should have.

“How long?”

“I cannot say.”

“You can.”

He swallowed. “Eleven minutes, perhaps. Ten. Maybe less.”

The room seemed to contract around us. Eleven minutes: the same interval I had forged into the maintenance log, the same number that had sent Tomas Reed to prison.

“Why lie?”

“Because Elias ordered me to.”

“And you obeyed.”

“I was a physician at Vale House. He owned the practice, the instruments, the charitable fund that kept half the coast alive. He told me that if the report suggested negligence, the authorities would seize the station, the workers would be blamed, and the families would receive nothing.”

“Did you believe him?”

“I believed I was afraid.”

That was the first honest thing anyone had said since Elias’s clock stopped.

“Was there another person in the tunnels?”

Frost looked at me then. His face had gone pale beneath the gray of his beard.

“There was another voice.”

“Whose?”

“I don’t know.”

“You heard it.”

“I heard a man shouting. Liora was shouting too. The machinery was screaming. Water was coming through the lower channels.” He rubbed one thumb across the silver handle of his cane. “I saw her hand once. That is all. She was alive when the water took her under.”

“Did Elias know?”

“Yes.”

“And he still made you call it an accident?”

“He made all of us call it an accident.”

The machinery beneath us gave a sudden clank. Frost flinched, and his cane struck the floor.

I leaned closer. “What did Liora find?”

“Drawings, I think. Old regulator plans. She had become convinced Elias had stolen other people’s work and fitted it together in this house.”

“Had he?”

Frost’s silence answered.

A knock sounded at the door. Pike stood there, impatient.

“Your time,” he said.

Frost rose. At the threshold, he paused.

“Miss Venn,” he said quietly, “there are accidents, and there are deaths arranged to resemble them. The difference is usually found in what someone has chosen to omit.”

I thought of an eleven-minute omission.

Then he went back to the hall.

Nora Bell was next. She had been Elias’s secretary for six years and wore her fear like a formal garment: buttoned to the throat, sleeves neat, hands folded.

I took her into the small library. The shelves leaned inward as if the books themselves were listening.

“You warned Elias that Liora had found something,” I said.

“I warned him that Liora was angry.”

“Those are not the same thing.”

“She was always angry near the end.”

“Why?”

Nora stared at a row of leather-bound account books. “Because she intended to leave.”

“Leave Blackwater?”

“Leave Elias. Leave the house. Leave the work.” Her mouth tightened. “She had arranged passage on a cargo steamer out of Rotterdam. She was going to publish the regulator designs and the correspondence proving Elias had taken them.”

“Whose designs?”

“Several inventors’. Her father’s most of all.”

“Why did you help conceal her letters?”

Nora’s eyes flashed. “I did not conceal them from her. I concealed them from Elias.”

“That is a distinction you should explain to Inspector Pike.”

“I will explain nothing to him until I know whether he intends to protect the truth or merely write a cleaner report than the last one.”

The rebuke was aimed at me, though she did not say my name.

I accepted it. “What did you hear in the tidal tunnels?”

Nora looked toward the library door. “Liora arguing with someone.”

“A man?”

“Yes.”

“You recognized the voice.”

Her expression changed—not fear now, but calculation.

“I heard only a few words.”

“What words?”

“‘You promised.’ And Liora said, ‘He will know.’”

“Who was the man?”

“I don’t know.”

“You heard the voice.”

She rose abruptly. “The storm is worsening.”

“That does not make a voice unfamiliar.”

“No,” she said. “It makes memory unreliable.”

She slipped past me and returned to the hall before Pike could call her back.

Ada Quill had been waiting beside the tall cabinet where Elias kept his patent models. She had one hand pressed against the opposite palm, hiding the red mark I had noticed earlier.

I brought her into the dining room. The table still held the remains of dinner: silver cooling under candlelight, wine glasses tremoring with every pulse of the storm.

“You searched the display room,” I said.

“Yes.”

“For proof that Elias stole your father’s work.”

“For proof that he stole more than the perpetual-motion design.”

“Did you find it?”

“I found what he wanted me to find.”

That stopped me. “Meaning?”

Ada drew a folded paper from her pocket. “Martin Pell’s regulator core. Or part of it. Elias had incorporated the design into the pressure governors beneath this house.”

“You’re certain?”

“My father built the first working model when I was seventeen. I watched him file the teeth by hand. I know the geometry.”

She unfolded the paper. It showed a cross-section of a valve assembly, annotated in a fine, cramped script.

“The regulator does not merely control pressure,” she said. “It anticipates it. That was my father’s innovation. Elias took the principle and made it large enough to run his entire estate.”

“Could it be used to cause Liora’s death?”

“If someone reversed the sequence, yes. The pressure would build in the lower pipes, then release all at once through the emergency gantry.”

“And the machine would appear to fail.”

“Precisely.”

“Could your father have done it?”

“He was dead.”

“Could you?”

Ada’s laugh was soft and bitter. “I could do it better than whoever did. That is not an admission.”

I glanced at the red mark on her palm. “What happened?”

“I cut myself on a broken spring.”

“Where?”

“In the display room.”

“Why conceal it?”

“Because everyone in this house is watching everyone else for blood.”

She refolded the plan. “Liora meant to expose Elias. She told me she had found the original regulator notation in the tunnels. She said the machine had been altered after my father’s death.”

“Did she name the person who altered it?”

Ada’s fingers closed over the paper.

“No.”

The lie was small, but it was there.

Before I could press her, Pike appeared again. “Sable.”

Victor Sable met me in the passage outside the wine cellar, where the air smelled of wet stone and spilled brandy. His cuff still bore the dark smear of grease. He kept turning that arm inward, as though the stain might accuse him if it faced the light.

“You handled payments for Elias,” I said.

“Investments.”

“Payments to inspectors. A solicitor. The Reed family.”

His eyes hardened. “You have been reading ledgers.”

“Someone had to.”

“Elias directed the transfers. I executed them.”

“To conceal Liora’s death?”

“To prevent a public scandal.”

“You paid people to keep quiet.”

“I paid people to avoid panic.”

“And Tomas Reed?”

Sable’s jaw worked. “Reed was a convenient target.”

The words came without ceremony. I felt the old room inside me open—the office three years ago, my own handwriting, the false maintenance time, the certainty with which I had made a man’s life fit the shape of my brother’s absence.

“What did you pay his family for?”

“Nothing directly. Elias arranged a solicitor. There was a settlement.”

“After Reed went to prison.”

Sable looked away.

“Did Elias order the forged log?”

“No.”

It was the first answer he gave too quickly.

“Did he know it was false?”

“He suspected.”

“Then why let Reed hang for it?”

“Because your evidence served his purpose.”

The storm boomed against the house. For a moment, the cellar shelves shuddered.

Sable lowered his voice. “You think I killed him because I moved money. Perhaps I did worse things than murder. That is how these matters work. The man who pays is blamed for the death; the man who turns the machine receives the benefit.”

“Who turned the machine?”

He studied me. “You should ask the mechanics.”

When I returned to the hall, Pike was speaking to Rook. The inspector’s hand rested on the evidence case containing the screwdriver.

“You said you never went below the east stairs,” Pike was saying.

“I said I did not go into the tidal station.”

“You were seen near the stairs.”

“I checked the pressure gauge.”

“By whom?”

“By me.”

Rook looked at me as I approached. There was no surprise in his expression. Only interest.

Pike gestured toward the servants’ corridor. “Take him there.”

The corridor was narrow, lined with copper pipes that trembled against the walls. We stopped beneath a brass speaking tube. The house seemed to breathe around us.

I faced Rook. “Tell me about Liora.”

“Which version?”

“The one that killed her.”

He gave a humorless smile. “You already know the official version.”

“I know it was false.”

“Then you know more than most.”

“You worked at the tidal station.”

“I maintained the pumps.”

“And the regulators.”

“When Elias permitted it.”

“Did you alter the machine?”

Rook’s eyes went to the pipe above my shoulder. “A regulator is altered every time it is adjusted.”

“Did you reverse it?”

“No.”

“Did you see Liora that night?”

“No.”

“Did you hear her arguing with a man?”

He looked at me then. “Yes.”

The admission tightened my throat. “Who?”

“I couldn’t see his face.”

“But you knew his voice.”

“I knew the voice.”

“Whose?”

Rook’s gaze held mine, and something almost like pity entered it.

“Jonah Venn’s.”

The pipe above us clicked as pressure shifted somewhere in the walls.

I heard the words, but they did not become meaning at once. Jonah had been the reason I altered the log. Jonah had been the reason I believed every version that let me place him somewhere else.

“You’re lying.”

“I have no reason to protect him.”

“You have every reason to destroy me.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“What was he doing there?”

Rook’s mouth flattened. “He helped install the prototype regulator. Elias hired him because Jonah understood the electrical controls better than any of us. Liora found out that the core had been stolen. She intended to expose Elias, and Jonah knew it.”

“Jonah would not hurt her.”

“I didn’t say he did.”

“You said his voice was there.”

“It was.”

“Doing what?”

“Arguing. Begging, perhaps. The machinery drowned most of it.”

I stepped closer. “You saw him?”

“Not clearly.”

“Then how can you be certain?”

“Because he called her by name. Because I had heard him in the workshop before. Because afterward he came to me and asked whether the regulator could be made to fail without leaving a mark.”

The corridor tilted. I put one hand against the wall.

Rook continued softly. “He said he was trying to save her.”

“And did he?”

“No.”

A door slammed somewhere deeper in the house. Pike appeared at the end of the corridor, one hand near his revolver.

“What did he say?” the inspector asked.

I turned toward him, but Rook answered first.

“I told her Jonah was in the tunnels.”

Pike’s face changed—not surprise. Confirmation of a suspicion he had been carrying longer than I knew.

“Did he cause the accident?” Pike asked.

Rook looked at me. “Ask his sister. She falsified the time.”

The words cut deeper than his accusation could have.

Pike came nearer. “Mara?”

I kept my eyes on the copper pipe. Inside it, water moved with a low, urgent murmur.
